newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain braces for labour reform battle.
newsitem.headline: Spain braces for labour reform battle.

text.p: Spain, plagued by unemployment at twice the European Union average, will press unions and employers for extensive labour market reform before a currency union in 1999 restricts the government's room to maneouvre.

Reform talks between unions and employers are due to begin in the first few weeks of 1997, but the conservative Popular Party government is already itchy and has threatened to intervene if the change is not radical enough.

"The government cannot be held apart from the terms of the agreement. An agreement where everything remains as is would not be sufficient," Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar said at an economic summit last week.
Aznar recently declared 1997 "The Year of the Job" in a bid to tame 22 percent unemployment.

The stakes are high and time is running out, analysts argue, fearing Spain's current labour framework is ill-suited to cope with monetary union and mass unemployment may result if reform doesn't come soon.
Up until now, Spain has often used peseta devaluations to cushion any loss of its competitive edge in downturns. But that recourse will no longer exist once the common currency is established.
The rigid, inefficient labour market will then have to cope.

"(In the case of recession) the effect will be more intense if reforms are not carried out because it won't be possible to devalue," Jose Luis Feito, Spanish envoy to the Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development, said last month.
"...If there is no reform of the labour market, competitivity will be lost and there will be adjustment," he added.
In large part, the needed reforms are the unpleasant side effect of the last labour law revision.
The 1994 reform, which introduced new specialised contracts for apprenticeships, internships and temporary work, was designed to:
- Ease labour market entry for young workers through new types of contracts
- Reduce restrictions on firing for economic causes
- Ensure that temporary contracts are for work that is indeed temporary.
But detractors say the changes institutionalised the split between permanent and temporary work, and left unresolved the issue of the excessive costs of dismissal.

According to data from the National Statistics Institute employment survey, temporary contracts represented 34 percent of total salaried and wage earners in the first nine months of the year compared to 35.2 percent in the same period in 1995.
While the law expanded economic dismissal causes in exchange for 20 days per year of service instead of a mandatory 45 days, the courts have rejected many of the cases brought before them by firms.
Although at present there are no concrete plans for changes, the government is looking for a reduction in the number of types of contracts to three or four from the current 14.
"The precariousness (in the labour market) is insupportable. This precariousness must be converted into stability of employment," Labour Minister Javier Arenas told journalists on Friday.

In order to reduce the sharp division between fixed and temporary workers, the government could look to a lowering of dismissal costs. The mechanism could be an indemnisation agreed beforehand between worker and employer or maximum legal time limits to temporary contracts.
"We cannot continue to see a labour contract as a fight between workers and employers. We need to find new useful, agile formulas," Aznar said.
